title: Spot the repeats
prompt: Customer cities repeat across rows. Show each different city as city with a count as customers, to see what could become its own table. Replace the ___.

cases.name: Different data
cases.setupSql: DELETE FROM order_items; DELETE FROM orders; DELETE FROM products; DELETE FROM customers; INSERT INTO customers VALUES (7, 'Ravi', 'Oslo', 'ravi@mail.test', '2024-05-05'), (8, 'Sara', 'Lima', NULL, '2024-06-06'), (9, 'Tom', 'Oslo', NULL, '2024-07-07'); INSERT INTO products VALUES (7, 'Stool', 'Home', 40.0, 25.0), (8, 'Cup', 'Kitchen', 9.0, 2.0), (9, 'Ink', 'Stationery', 12.5, 6.0); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (11, 7, '2024-02-28', 'shipped'), (12, 8, '2024-03-01', 'pending'), (13, 7, '2024-03-31', 'cancelled'); INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (11, 7, 1, 4.0), (11, 8, 3, NULL), (12, 9, 2, NULL), (13, 8, 1, NULL);

solutions: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customers FROM customers GROUP BY city;

wrongSolutions.sql: SELECT name, COUNT(*) AS customers FROM customers GROUP BY name;

title: Extract a table
prompt: Create a table named cities with id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and name TEXT, filled with each different customer city. Let SQLite assign ids.

check.sql: SELECT name FROM cities ORDER BY name;

cases.name: Different data
cases.setupSql: DELETE FROM order_items; DELETE FROM orders; DELETE FROM products; DELETE FROM customers; INSERT INTO customers VALUES (7, 'Ravi', 'Oslo', 'ravi@mail.test', '2024-05-05'), (8, 'Sara', 'Lima', NULL, '2024-06-06'), (9, 'Tom', 'Oslo', NULL, '2024-07-07'); INSERT INTO products VALUES (7, 'Stool', 'Home', 40.0, 25.0), (8, 'Cup', 'Kitchen', 9.0, 2.0), (9, 'Ink', 'Stationery', 12.5, 6.0); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (11, 7, '2024-02-28', 'shipped'), (12, 8, '2024-03-01', 'pending'), (13, 7, '2024-03-31', 'cancelled'); INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (11, 7, 1, 4.0), (11, 8, 3, NULL), (12, 9, 2, NULL), (13, 8, 1, NULL);

solutions: CREATE TABLE cities (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); INSERT INTO cities (name) SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers;

wrongSolutions.sql: CREATE TABLE cities (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); INSERT INTO cities (name) SELECT city FROM customers;
CREATE TABLE cities (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);

title: Add the link
prompt: Add a city_id INTEGER column to customers, then create and fill cities as before, and set each customer's city_id from the matching row.
hints: ALTER, CREATE, INSERT, then UPDATE with a subquery.

check.sql: SELECT c.id, ci.name FROM customers c JOIN cities ci ON ci.id = c.city_id ORDER BY c.id;

cases.name: Different data
cases.setupSql: DELETE FROM order_items; DELETE FROM orders; DELETE FROM products; DELETE FROM customers; INSERT INTO customers VALUES (7, 'Ravi', 'Oslo', 'ravi@mail.test', '2024-05-05'), (8, 'Sara', 'Lima', NULL, '2024-06-06'), (9, 'Tom', 'Oslo', NULL, '2024-07-07'); INSERT INTO products VALUES (7, 'Stool', 'Home', 40.0, 25.0), (8, 'Cup', 'Kitchen', 9.0, 2.0), (9, 'Ink', 'Stationery', 12.5, 6.0); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (11, 7, '2024-02-28', 'shipped'), (12, 8, '2024-03-01', 'pending'), (13, 7, '2024-03-31', 'cancelled'); INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (11, 7, 1, 4.0), (11, 8, 3, NULL), (12, 9, 2, NULL), (13, 8, 1, NULL);

solutions: CREATE TABLE cities (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); INSERT INTO cities (name) SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers ORDER BY city; ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN city_id INTEGER; UPDATE customers SET city_id = (SELECT id FROM cities WHERE cities.name = customers.city);

wrongSolutions.sql: CREATE TABLE cities (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); INSERT INTO cities (name) SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers ORDER BY city; ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN city_id INTEGER;

CREATE TABLE cities (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); INSERT INTO cities (name) SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers ORDER BY city; ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN city_id INTEGER; UPDATE customers SET city_id = 1;

title: A linking table
prompt: Students take many clubs, and clubs have many students. Create club_members with student_id INTEGER, club_id INTEGER, and PRIMARY KEY (student_id, club_id).
hints: A composite primary key prevents repeat memberships.

check.sql: SELECT name, type, "notnull", pk FROM pragma_table_info('club_members') ORDER BY cid;

solutions: CREATE TABLE club_members (student_id INTEGER, club_id INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, club_id));

wrongSolutions.sql: CREATE TABLE club_members (student_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, club_id INTEGER);
wrongSolutions.why: A student could join just one club

wrongSolutions.sql: CREATE TABLE club_members (student_id INTEGER, club_id INTEGER);
wrongSolutions.why: No key, so memberships can repeat

title: One fact, one place
prompt: A course's subject is stored once, in courses. Using a join rather than a copied column, show each enrolment's id and subject.

cases.name: Different data
cases.setupSql: DELETE FROM enrolments; DELETE FROM courses; DELETE FROM students; INSERT INTO students VALUES (6, 'Femi', 9), (7, 'Gia', 9), (8, 'Hao', 10); INSERT INTO courses VALUES (5, 'Chemistry', 'Science'), (6, 'Drama', 'Arts'); INSERT INTO enrolments VALUES (11, 6, 5, 60, '2023-autumn'), (12, 6, 5, 60, '2024-spring'), (13, 7, 5, NULL, '2024-spring'), (14, 7, 6, 95, '2024-spring');

solutions: SELECT e.id, c.subject FROM enrolments e JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id;

wrongSolutions.sql: SELECT e.id, c.subject FROM enrolments e JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.student_id;
SELECT e.id, e.term AS subject FROM enrolments e;

title: Fix the duplicated fact
prompt: Marco moved to Milan, and his city must change in one place. This statement changes the wrong row. Fix it.

check.sql: SELECT id, city FROM customers ORDER BY id;

cases.name: Different data
cases.setupSql: DELETE FROM order_items; DELETE FROM orders; DELETE FROM products; DELETE FROM customers; INSERT INTO customers VALUES (7, 'Ravi', 'Oslo', 'ravi@mail.test', '2024-05-05'), (8, 'Sara', 'Lima', NULL, '2024-06-06'), (9, 'Tom', 'Oslo', NULL, '2024-07-07'); INSERT INTO products VALUES (7, 'Stool', 'Home', 40.0, 25.0), (8, 'Cup', 'Kitchen', 9.0, 2.0), (9, 'Ink', 'Stationery', 12.5, 6.0); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (11, 7, '2024-02-28', 'shipped'), (12, 8, '2024-03-01', 'pending'), (13, 7, '2024-03-31', 'cancelled'); INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (11, 7, 1, 4.0), (11, 8, 3, NULL), (12, 9, 2, NULL), (13, 8, 1, NULL); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (2, 'Marco', 'Rome', NULL, '2023-02-14');
